prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

After IVAN ALBRIGHT’s Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida She arrived as near to virginal as girls got in those days—i.e., young, the requisite dewy cheek flushed at its own daring. He had hoped for a little more edge. But she held the newspaper rolled like a scepter, his advertisement turned up to prove she was there solely at his bidding—and yet the gold band, the photographs ... a mother, then. He placed her in the old garden chair, the same one he went to evenings when the first tug on the cord sent the bulb swinging like the lamps in the medic’s tent over the wounded, swaddled shapes that moaned each time the Screaming Meemies let loose, their calculated shrieks so far away he thought of crickets—while all around him matted gauze and ether pricked up an itch so bad he could hardly sketch each clean curve of tissue opening.I shut my eyes, walk straight to it. Nothing special but it’s there, wicker fraying under my calming fingers.

After Ivan Albright’s *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida*

She arrived as near to virginal as girls came in those days—that is, young, with the requisite dewy cheek flushed at its own daring. He had hoped for a little more edge. But she held the newspaper rolled like a scepter, his advertisement turned upward to prove she was there solely at his bidding—and yet the gold band, the photographs… a mother, then. He placed her in the old garden chair, the same one to which he went in the evenings, when the first tug on the cord sent the bulb swinging like the lamps in the medic’s tent over the wounded, swaddled shapes that moaned each time the Screaming Meemies let loose, their calculated shrieks so far away he thought of crickets—while all around him, matted gauze and ether raised an itch so fierce he could hardly sketch each clean curve of tissue opening.

I shut my eyes and walk straight to it. Nothing special, but it is there: wicker fraying beneath my calming fingers.
outputs.L2:
After Ivan Albright’s *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida*

She came to him seeming almost as innocent as a girl could appear then: youthful, with the expected fresh cheek reddening as if embarrassed by its own boldness. He had wanted someone with a sharper quality. Still, she carried the newspaper rolled in her hand like a royal staff, his notice facing outward as evidence that she had come only because he had summoned her. Yet there was the wedding ring, and the photographs—so she was a mother.

He seated her in the old garden chair, the very chair he sought out in the evenings, when the first pull on the cord made the light bulb sway like the lamps in the medical tent above the injured, bundled figures who groaned whenever the Screaming Meemies began their deliberate howls. They sounded so distant to him that they brought crickets to mind, while around him the smell of ether and clotted gauze raised such an unbearable itch that he could barely draw the pure arcs of exposed tissue.

I close my eyes and go directly toward it. It is nothing remarkable, but it is present: wicker coming apart beneath my steadying hands.
outputs.L3:
Ida arrived in response to the advertisement, a young woman whose manner immediately suggested innocence and unease. She seemed self-conscious in the doorway, as if uncertain whether she belonged there or whether she had misunderstood what was expected of her. There was nothing bold or hardened about her appearance. On the contrary, she gave the impression of someone gentle and unprepared, someone who had come because she needed to, not because she was naturally suited to the situation.

The narrator had expected a very different kind of person. From the advertisement, or perhaps from his own assumptions about who would answer it, he had imagined someone tougher, someone with more edge and resilience. Ida did not match that image. Her softness, her hesitant movements, and her air of vulnerability made her seem almost out of place. Instead of the worldly, practical figure he had anticipated, she appeared fragile, exposed, and far younger in spirit than he had expected.

Small details, however, complicated this first impression. A gold band on her finger suggested marriage, or at least a past connection marked by commitment. The photographs she carried or kept with her hinted even more strongly at another life beyond the one she presented in that moment. They suggested that she was a mother, that somewhere outside this encounter there were children or family ties that shaped her circumstances. These objects gave her a quiet depth, revealing that her innocence did not mean she was untouched by responsibility or experience.

The narrator placed Ida in an old garden chair, a chair that already held a private significance for him. It was not merely a piece of furniture but part of his evening rituals, something associated with habit, reflection, and the slow passage of time. By seating her there, he brought her into a space marked by his own memories. The ordinary act of offering a chair became charged with association, as though Ida’s presence had disturbed something settled and familiar.

The chair, in particular, awakened memories from the war. It carried the narrator back to medical scenes crowded with wounded soldiers, where bodies lay under harsh lights and the air was filled with pain, urgency, and exhaustion. He remembered the glare of lamps, the strained faces, the sense of waiting and suffering, and beyond it all the distant sound of shelling. What should have been a simple domestic object became a trigger for recollection, linking the quiet present with the violence and trauma of the past. Ida’s arrival, and her placement in that chair, therefore opened not only a new encounter but also a passage into memories the narrator could not entirely leave behind.
outputs.L4:
The passage presents a fragmented, intensely visual meditation on memory, trauma, and artistic perception through an ekphrastic response to Ivan Albright’s painting. Rather than describing the artwork in a straightforward or orderly way, the text moves through broken images, shifting points of view, and layered associations. Its language lingers on surfaces, bodies, rooms, objects, and gestures, allowing each detail to become unstable and emotionally charged. What at first appears to be an act of looking at a painting gradually becomes an encounter with the past, especially with the lingering effects of wartime experience.

Through vivid and often unsettling imagery, the passage suggests that ordinary things are never merely ordinary. Furniture, clothing, skin, tools, and domestic spaces seem to hold traces of violence, loss, and survival. Human figures appear not only as subjects within an artwork but also as witnesses, victims, makers, and memories. The boundaries between the painter, the viewer, and the figures being observed begin to blur, creating a sense that perception itself has been altered by trauma.

The fragmented structure reflects the difficulty of representing painful memory directly. Instead of offering a clear narrative, the passage allows images to accumulate and collide, as trauma often returns in flashes, repetitions, and distortions. The act of looking becomes inseparable from remembering, and the act of artistic creation becomes a way of confronting what cannot be easily spoken. In this way, the passage reveals how the past persists beneath the surface of visual experience. It shows that art does not simply preserve appearances; it exposes the hidden pressures of history, memory, and suffering that continue to inhabit both objects and bodies.

After the storm had passed, IVAN stood alone beneath the pale morning sky, watching the last clouds drift beyond the hills. The town was quiet, as if the world were holding its breath. Windows were boarded, streets were wet, and the old ALBRIGHT house at the edge of the road seemed to glow faintly in the returning sunlight.

IVAN had always heard stories about the ALBRIGHT family—tales of hidden letters, vanished travelers, and a locked room no one had opened in decades. After years of ignoring the rumors, he finally felt drawn to the place. Something about that morning made the impossible seem within reach.

He stepped through the broken gate and approached the front door. After one deep breath, IVAN raised his hand and knocked. To his surprise, the door slowly opened, revealing a hallway filled with dust, silence, and secrets waiting to be found.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short ekphrastic prose poem titled “After IVAN ALBRIGHT’s Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida,” blending description of the painting with a disturbed painter’s imagined inner monologue and a sudden first-person ending.
counterfactuals.output:
**After IVAN ALBRIGHT’s *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida***

She sits like a wound taught to wear satin: greenish flesh, bruised lace, a little kingdom of powder, comb, flower, coin, and mirror collapsing around her. Every surface remembers rot. The chair gnaws her hips. Her hands, jeweled and swollen, pose as if beauty might still answer to command.

Paint her slower, says the painter inside the paint. Give every pore its verdict. Let the silk sour. Let the eyelid sag like a curtain over a theater where no one applauded. Do not spare the rose, the ribbon, the mouth insisting it was kissed. A soul came into the world called Ida—yes—but who called it, and why did it stay?

The room thickens. The mirror refuses rescue. Time is not passing here; it is feeding.

I lean closer, and her face begins to arrange itself into mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary flash fiction piece inspired by Ivan Albright’s painting Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida, using dense, unsettling imagery, references to WWI trauma, and ending with the narrator touching an old wicker garden chair.
counterfactuals.output:
When Ida arrived, the midwife said the room filled with the smell of damp pennies and cut chrysanthemums. My mother, feverish in the brass bed, laughed because she thought the child had come already dead and polished, an artifact dredged from under the sea. But Ida opened her eyes—two bruised plums in milk—and the wallpaper began to peel in long, tongue-colored strips.

I was six then, old enough to remember the winter lice in my father’s puttees, the letters edged black, the way men came home from France walking as if they were carrying their own graves under their coats. My father returned with no visible wound, which made everyone nervous. He sat at supper and chewed each bite thirty times, his jaw clicking like a rifle bolt. At night he cried out for a boy named Mulligan and kicked the bedstead until the plaster sifted down. He had learned in the trenches that mud could swallow a man tenderly, like a mother, leaving only the helmet to prove there had been a head.

Ida grew in that house as mold grows behind a mirror.

By twelve she had the face of an old woman who had spent her life being born. Her skin held light badly; it curdled there in yellow pools. She sat for hours at my mother’s dressing table, where the silver-backed brushes bloomed green at the handles and the powder puff resembled a skinned mouse. She combed her hair until it snapped and shivered down the front of her dress. She opened jars of cold cream and touched the white fat to her cheeks as if embalming herself for a dance no one had invited her to attend.

“Pretty,” she would say, not as a question or a hope, but as an accusation.

Outside, boys drilled in the schoolyard with broomsticks, preparing for the next war their fathers had already brought home inside them. The town band played marches on Decoration Day, and the veterans flinched at the cymbals. My father stood among them in his too-tight uniform, medals trembling on his breast like trapped insects. Ida watched from the parlor window, her fingers leaving wet half-moons on the glass. She loved ceremonies of damage: parades, funerals, the opening of canned meat, the cracking of walnuts with a hammer.

The summer she turned twenty, a photographer came through town taking portraits of respectable families. My mother insisted Ida sit for one. She laced her into a dress the color of old teeth and fastened a brooch at her throat, a cameo woman with no eyes. Ida sat upright beneath the skylight while the photographer vanished under his black cloth. I remember the flash: a white explosion, the room briefly no room at all but a field after shellfire—curtains lifted, flowers decapitated, everyone’s shadow burned against the wall.

My father fell to the floor and crawled under the table.

Ida did not move. In the photograph, when it came, her hands rested in her lap like two pale animals that had been trapped and had stopped struggling. Behind her, the painted backdrop showed a garden with roses, urns, a path leading nowhere. She had never looked more alive. She had never looked more ruined.

Years later, after my mother died and my father mistook the cellar for a dugout and would not come up for three days, Ida began to rot in earnest. Not with disease, the doctor said, though he washed his hands in our kitchen sink until the skin reddened and split. It was simply that time loved her too much. It gathered in the hollows of her collarbones, nested beneath her eyes, thickened her ankles, sugared her breath. She painted her mouth red every morning, wider than a mouth should go, and smiled at herself in the mirror as if recognizing an enemy across no-man’s-land.

“You can hear them under the floor,” she told me once.

“Who?”

“The ones who didn’t finish dying.”

I listened. The pipes ticked. A beetle worried the baseboard. Somewhere beyond the wall, my father whispered coordinates to God.

When Ida finally left the house, she wore gloves though it was August. She crossed the yard to the dead garden where the arbor had collapsed under grapes gone black and sweet with wasps. The chair was there, as it had been since before the war, before Ida, before my father learned the music of artillery: a wicker garden chair, gray with weather, its arms unraveled, its seat sagging like a mouth trying to speak.

She sat in it and faced the sun. All afternoon she diminished by degrees. Not disappeared—nothing so merciful. She became more exactly herself: powder, stain, lace, bone, breath held too long in a closed room. By evening the chair was empty except for the imprint of her weight and one glove, stiffened at the fingers as though still gripping the world.

I did not call anyone. The house behind me clicked and settled, full of medals, mirrors, boots, jars, the yellowed photograph of Ida in her counterfeit garden. The earth smelled of rust and crushed roses. I stepped closer, hearing in the wicker the faint dry chatter of bones, rifles, summer insects, teeth.

Now I am touching an old wicker garden chair.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a paragraph in a modernist, psychologically intense style that begins “After IVAN ALBRIGHT’s Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida” and imagines the artist arranging Ida in his studio while memories of a medic’s tent intrude.
counterfactuals.output: After IVAN ALBRIGHT’s *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida*, he arranged her in the studio as one might arrange evidence: the slack purse, the hat like a wilted verdict, the powdered face already losing its argument with the flesh beneath. Light crawled over her in patches, surgical and accusing, and the room seemed to thicken with the odor of oil, dust, old cloth—until it was not the studio but the medic’s tent again, canvas sweating in the heat, lanterns trembling over torn uniforms, bodies opened to their astonishing interiors. He touched the brush to her cheek and saw gauze darken; he mixed gray into rose and heard a man calling for water, for mother, for God, each name collapsing into the same wet syllable. Ida sat there, monumental in her exhaustion, and he understood that beauty was not a rescue but an exposure, a merciless patience: the soul forced outward through pores, wrinkles, bruised knuckles, the little shine of vanity surviving amid ruin. So he painted her as if dressing a wound that would not close.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an ekphrastic response to Albright’s Ida painting: make it lyrical, grotesque, and fragmented, with a young mother answering an advertisement, a newspaper, photographs, a gold band, and a wartime flashback involving “Screaming Meemies.”
counterfactuals.output:
She comes because the newspaper says:

**WANTED: WOMAN TO SIT.  
Age no matter. Beauty no object.  
Hourly wage. Bring patience.**

So she brings the baby’s milk on her dress,  
brings one glove and not the other,  
brings the damp little purse  
with its mouth of snapped brass.

The studio smells of turpentine, dust,  
old apples going brown in a bowl.  
On the wall, photographs:  
a girl with her hair pinned like a promise,  
a soldier blurred at the shoulder,  
a family arranged in their Sunday stiffness,  
all those paper faces shining  
as if already dead.

Ida sits.

Her young body has been told to become old.  
The chair takes her in like a swamp.  
Her knees shine. Her stockings sag.  
Her hands are roots washed up from a graveyard,  
knuckles knobbed and bluish,  
fingers remembering soap, diapers, bread, coal smoke.

On one finger, the gold band.

Small sun.  
Little shackle.  
Halo fallen to the hand.

She turns it when she is nervous—  
round and round,  
as though marriage were a screw  
and she might loosen herself from it.

The painter looks.  
Looks harder.

He finds the green under the skin,  
the yellow in the whites of the eyes,  
the soft collapse under the chin  
where time has already set up house.  
He paints each pore like a warning bell.  
He paints the mouth as if it has tasted pennies.  
He paints her beauty rotting forward,  
not gone, not spared,  
but opening—  
a flower made of meat.

Baby at home.  
Rent due.  
Husband gone two weeks.  
Or three.  
The calendar a cracked plate.

She hears, in the street, a truck backfire—  
and suddenly it is France again,  
or the story of France,  
or the place he carried in his sleep:

night split open,  
mud sucking boots,  
the sky stitched with fire,  
and the men saying **Screaming Meemies**  
for the rockets that came down howling,  
that animal choir,  
that iron nursery song.

He had told her once, drunk,  
how the sound arrived before death,  
how it curled inside the teeth.  
How a man could become a photograph  
before he hit the ground.

In the studio, the camera’s glass eye glints.  
In the newspaper, yesterday’s war yellows.  
In her lap, her hands lie still  
as abandoned gloves.

Ida, Ida—  
advertisement answered,  
face delivered,  
life paid by the hour.

The painter gives her lace, a chair, a terrible mirror.  
Gives her every minute at once.  
Girl-wife, mother, widow-in-advance.  
Her flesh keeps the receipt.

Outside, the city proceeds:  
cars cough, pigeons lift,  
someone sells oranges from a crate.

Inside, she blooms into ruin.

The gold band holds.  
The photographs watch.  
The newspaper folds itself shut.

And from far off—  
or from under the paint—  
the Screaming Meemies begin again,  
thin as whistles,  
bright as knives,  
calling every young thing  
by its future name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose-poem vignette inspired by Ivan Albright, shifting from third-person narration about a model named Ida to a brief first-person meditation; include an old garden chair, a swinging bulb, ether, gauze, and the phrase “I shut my eyes, walk straight to it.”
counterfactuals.output:
Ida sits where the painter has left her, in the old garden chair dragged indoors from some vanished summer, its wicker hips unraveling, its legs freckled with rust. Above her, a swinging bulb worries the room into motion, light passing over her face like a hand unsure whether to bless or bruise. Everything around her has the patience of decay: the basin with its dull rim, the mirror clouded as if it had breathed in ether, the gauze folded on the table like a small, surrendered flag.

She does not pose so much as persist. Her dress gathers at the knees in tired tributaries. Her hands, heavy and lucid, rest in her lap with the authority of roots. The painter studies every pore as if it were a doorway, every fold as if time had written there in a language too intimate to translate. Ida’s body becomes a room inside the room, furnished with waiting, lit by the bulb’s frail pendulum, sweetened and sickened by the medicinal air.

I think of how flesh is never still, even in stillness; how the self rises through us, mottled, faithful, difficult. There is a place in the dark where the figure remains after the lamp goes out. I shut my eyes, walk straight to it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
